introduction-the-saas-margin-crisis.core: SaaS companies can grow revenue while losing money if each customer costs more to serve than they pay. Cost per tenant reveals which customers and tiers are profitable.

first_principles.problem: Revenue is booming, but gross margin is falling because a few heavy tenants consume most of the infrastructure.
derivation: Fix it through **pricing, limits or architecture**.

analogy.title: A lemonade stand with a refill problem
analogy.story: Selling cups at $2 is fine until some customers take five free refills.
analogy.breaks: Strategic customers may be worth serving at low margin, but do it deliberately.

check.q: Why can SaaS revenue growth hide a margin problem?
check.a: If heavy customers cost more to serve than they pay, more revenue brings proportionally more cost.

architecture-dictates-cost-visibility.core: Tenant isolation decides how easy cost attribution is. Silo (dedicated resources per tenant) is easy to tag but expensive, pool (shared everything) is efficient but needs metering, and bridge or hybrid sits between them.

first_principles.problem: With a fully pooled database, there's no 'tenant A database' to read costs from.
truths: Dedicated resources map directly to bills.
Isolation level affects both cost and visibility.
derivation: **Pool**: meter usage per tenant → allocate shared cost.

analogy.title: Detached houses vs. an apartment block
analogy.story: Each house has its own meter; apartments share utilities that must be split by usage.
analogy.breaks: Silo per tenant can make small tenants unprofitable because of fixed overhead.

example.title: A tiered isolation strategy

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Visibility and cost match what each tier pays.

example.outcome: architecture chosen with cost visibility in mind.

check.q: Why is cost per tenant harder to calculate in a pooled architecture?
check.a: Resources are shared, so there's nothing per-tenant to tag; usage must be metered and costs allocated.

calculating-cost-in-a-pooled-model.core: In pooled systems, emit per-tenant consumption metrics (requests, CPU-seconds, storage GB, queries) and allocate each shared resource's cost in proportion to each tenant's share of its driver.

first_principles.problem: A $50k/month shared cluster and database can't be attributed to tenants without data.
truths: Applications know which tenant made each request.
derivation: **Instrument**: tag metrics and logs with tenant_id.
**Choose a driver** per resource (DB: query time; storage: GB; compute: CPU-seconds).

analogy.title: Splitting a shared office's electricity by desk usage meters
analogy.story: Each desk logs its power draw, and the bill is split accordingly.
analogy.breaks: Choosing a single driver for a multi-dimensional resource is an approximation.

example.title: Allocating a shared Postgres

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each tenant's share of the $12k database becomes visible.

example.outcome: credible cost per tenant in shared systems.

check.q: What's needed to allocate pooled costs to tenants?
check.a: Per-tenant consumption metrics for each shared resource's cost driver.

tiered-pricing-strategy-and-the-free-tie.core: Price tiers must exceed their cost to serve, with limits that keep heavy usage on higher tiers. Free tiers are customer acquisition cost: budget them, cap them, and make sure they convert.

first_principles.problem: A generous free tier attracts heavy users who never upgrade, and infrastructure costs explode.
truths: Every tier has a cost profile.
derivation: Set each tier's **price above cost to serve** plus margin.
Treat free as **CAC** with conversion targets.

analogy.title: A gym's pricing
analogy.story: Off-peak memberships are cheap because those members use less; an unlimited free trial with no end brings in people who never pay.
analogy.breaks: Limits that are too strict hurt adoption, so balance growth against cost.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The free tier becomes an affordable funnel.

check.q: Why treat a free tier as customer acquisition cost?
check.a: Its infrastructure cost is spent to acquire future paying customers, so it needs budgets and conversion targets.

key-saas-unit-economics-metrics.core: Cost per tenant feeds the standard SaaS metrics: gross margin, CAC, LTV (lifetime value), the LTV:CAC ratio (aim for >3), payback period and net revenue retention. Infrastructure efficiency shows up directly in LTV.

first_principles.problem: Engineering cost metrics don't connect to the metrics executives and investors use.
truths: Investors benchmark against standard SaaS metrics.

analogy.title: A subscription box business
analogy.story: You need to know how much each subscriber pays over their lifetime, minus what each box costs, versus what it cost to sign them up.
analogy.breaks: These are simplified formulas, and real models account for expansion and discounting.

example.title: How a COGS cut raises LTV

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Engineering efficiency improves the company's core economics.

example.outcome: infrastructure cost tied to SaaS valuation metrics.

check.q: How does reducing cost per tenant affect LTV?
check.a: It raises gross margin, which increases lifetime value per customer.
